notes: Attorney General unduly lenient sentence reference; court grants leave but declines to increase sentence.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference No 98: unduly lenient sentence for indecent assault on child
key_facts: The offender was convicted after trial of indecently assaulting a 9-year-old boy while the victim's father was briefly absent from a landscaping site.
He had a prior 6-year extended sentence for indecent assault on a 13-year-old girl and committed the offence while still on licence.
Mr Recorder Grant initially imposed a 4-year extended sentence with a 12-month custodial term, then reconvened under the slip rule and ordered 2 years of the outstanding balance to be served first.
The Attorney General referred the 12-month custodial term as unduly lenient given the victim's age, compulsion, impact, lack of remorse and high risk assessment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 for leave to refer an unduly lenient sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to refer was granted, but the Court of Appeal declined to interfere with the sentence despite finding the 12-month custodial term unduly lenient, bearing in mind double jeopardy and the defensive nature of the reference.
enrichment.ratio: On an unduly lenient sentence reference the court may grant leave yet decline to increase a sentence where interference would require a lower effective term than would otherwise be appropriate and where the Attorney General should not launch defensive references.
legal_issues: Whether the 12-month custodial term was unduly lenient for indecent assault on a young child by a repeat offender on licence
Whether the Court of Appeal should increase the sentence on a defensive Attorney General reference
Application of the four sentencing dimensions in child indecent assault cases
Appropriate use of extended sentences and recall of outstanding balance
linked_authorities: Attorney-General's References Nos 37, 38 etc [2004] 1 Cr App R(S) 499
R v Nelson [2002] 1 Cr App R(S) 565

confidence.notes: Facts, aggravating features and the court's explicit non-interference despite undue lenience are clearly recorded.

notes: Detailed assessment appeal on bankruptcy dismissal costs; Lownds proportionality ruling upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Ross v Stonewood: appeal from detailed assessment of bankruptcy costs
key_facts: Mr Ross successfully appealed dismissal of a Stonewood bankruptcy petition based on a £40,000 judgment debt, with the Court of Appeal ordering 75% of his costs on the standard basis.
Dass Solicitors presented bills totalling over £400,000 after complex litigation involving two bankruptcies, multiple Court of Appeal hearings and voluminous historical documents.
Costs Judge Rogers applied the Lownds two-stage approach, ruled costs disproportionate on their face and assessed between-parties costs at about £64,000 and LSC costs at about £97,000.
Lord Woolf CJ, sitting with assessors, dismissed appeals against the preliminary proportionality ruling, the Grade 1 charging rate, document-reading hours and Mr Levy's reduced counsel fees.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from a detailed assessment of costs following successful dismissal of a bankruptcy petition.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the preliminary disproportionality ruling, hourly rate of £190, disallowance of unexplained document hours and reduction of counsel fees were all upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A costs judge may properly make a preliminary Lownds disproportionality ruling at the outset of assessment without a CPR 44.5(3) checklist; on that basis the receiving party must justify each item as necessary and reasonable, and unexplained high counsel fees may be disallowed even where time was spent.
legal_issues: Whether Costs Judge Rogers erred in his preliminary Lownds disproportionality ruling
Whether an 85% enhancement over the Birmingham guideline rate was reasonable
Whether over 100 hours preparing Court of Appeal bundles were necessary
Whether counsel fees were wrongly reduced for lack of an Armitage v Nurse memorandum
linked_authorities: Lownds v Home Office [2002] 1 WLR 1311
Armitage v Nurse [2000] Costs LR 231
G v G (Minors: Custody Appeal) [1985] 1 WLR 647

notes: Charlotte Wyatt end-of-life treatment judgment; ventilation refused as not in best interests.

enrichment.short_title: Portsmouth NHS Trust v Wyatt: withholding ventilation for profoundly disabled infant
key_facts: Charlotte Wyatt was born at 26 weeks with chronic respiratory and kidney failure and profound irreversible brain damage leaving her blind, deaf and incapable of voluntary movement.
Unanimous medical evidence was that she experienced pain, would almost certainly need ventilation if she deteriorated further, and had minimal prospects of surviving 12 months.
Her parents sought elective tracheostomy and ventilation; doctors and the guardian opposed further aggressive treatment as not in her best interests.
The case was heard in public before a court of Lord Hoffman, Lord Donaldson and Lord Taylor.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application by the NHS trust for declaratory relief resolving disagreement with parents over life-prolonging treatment for a seriously ill infant.
enrichment.outcome: The court held that further invasive ventilation or similar aggressive treatment was not in Charlotte's best interests and granted permissive relief authorising doctors not to ventilate if parents and clinicians disagreed.
enrichment.ratio: Best interests in withholding treatment cases requires a generous welfare balance including sanctity of life, dignity and prospects of a good death; where treatment would be intolerable to the child and offer no commensurate benefit, the court may authorise clinicians not to provide it despite parental wishes.
legal_issues: Whether artificial ventilation and tracheostomy were in Charlotte Wyatt's best interests
How parental views and guardian recommendations should be weighed
Application of the strong presumption in favour of prolonging life
Whether permissive declaratory relief was appropriate
linked_authorities: Airedale NHS Trust v Bland [1993] AC 789
In re J (a Minor) (Wardship: Medical treatment) [1991] Fam 33
R (Burke) v GMC [2004] EWHC 1879 (Admin)

notes: Bahamas extradition habeas corpus; dual ATP, cross-examination and PACE admissibility issues rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Fernandes: extradition committal and PACE admissibility on cruise ship

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: Three cruise-ship waiters were committed for extradition to the Bahamas for unlawful sexual intercourse with a 14-year-old passenger.
The case depended on the complainant's account and admissions obtained by the ship's security director without PACE caution, adviser or contemporaneous notes.
The Secretary of State issued two authorities to proceed on intra- and extra-territorial bases; the district judge refused cross-examination of the vulnerable complainant.
Without Mr Swift's evidence there was insufficient identification evidence against any applicant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for habeas corpus challenging committal to await extradition to the Bahamas after Bow Street extradition proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: All three habeas corpus applications were dismissed; dual authorities to proceed were valid, refusal to cross-examine was lawful, and Mr Swift's interview evidence was admissible.
enrichment.ratio: In extradition committal proceedings Code C and section 76 apply only in rare cases where evidence would outrage civilised values; comity and reciprocity constrain exclusion at the committal stage, and a district judge may protect a vulnerable witness from cross-examination where a prima facie case is otherwise made out.
legal_issues: Whether two concurrent authorities to proceed were mutually inconsistent
Whether the district judge erred in refusing cross-examination of the complainant
Whether ship security admissions were inadmissible under sections 76 or 78 of PACE
Whether Code C applied to interviews on a Bahamian-registered vessel
linked_authorities: R v Governor of Brixton Prison, ex p Levin [1997] AC 741
R (Proulx) v Governor of Brixton Prison [2001] 1 All ER 57
R (Rottman) v Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police [2002] 2 AC 692

notes: Preston equal pay TUPE limitation appeal; time runs from transfer not transferee termination.

enrichment.short_title: Powerhouse Retail: TUPE transferor equal pay limitation period
key_facts: Part-time electricity industry workers denied access to occupational pension schemes brought equal pay claims in the Preston litigation.
Following privatisation their employment transferred under TUPE in 1992 but pension rights were excluded by Regulation 7.
Claims were brought more than six months after the TUPE transfer while the claimants remained employed by the transferee.
It was accepted that any claim lay against the transferor for pre-transfer periods.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on when section 2(4) of the Equal Pay Act 1970 begins to run against a TUPE transferor.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; time runs from the date of the TUPE transfer, not from termination of employment with the transferee.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 7 removes pension terms from the continuing contract with the transferee, so the post-transfer contract shorn of pension rights is not the specific contract giving rise to the pension equal pay claim; the transferor contract terminated on transfer and the six-month limitation period began then.
legal_issues: Whether 'employed in the employment' in section 2(4) continues while the employee remains with the transferee
Effect of TUPE Regulations 5 and 7 on pension equal pay claims
Whether Young and Davitt assist the claimants
Legal certainty for transferors after TUPE transfers
linked_authorities: Preston v Wolverhampton Healthcare NHS Trust (No.2) [2001] ICR 217 (HL)
National Power plc v Young [2001] ICR 328
Nokes v Doncaster Amalgamated Collieries [1940] AC 1014

notes: Bank guarantee interest appeal; late amendment for compound contractual interest allowed.

enrichment.short_title: Habib Bank v Dawood: amendment to claim compound contractual interest
key_facts: Mr Dawood guaranteed up to £300,000 of Barry McColgan's indebtedness to Habib Bank under a 1989 guarantee.
After formal demand the bank issued proceedings in 1993 claiming principal, statutory interest and continuing interest, obtaining liability judgment for £300,000 in 2002.
During a reserved hearing on interest the bank sought late permission to amend to claim compound contractual interest rather than section 35A statutory interest.
Judge Hegarty refused amendment and later struck out a second action for compound interest; the guarantor did not appear on appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Mercantile Court refusals to permit amendment for compound contractual interest and to allow a second claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; permission to amend granted and judgment entered for £147,607.51 compound interest, with a short window for the defendant to challenge calculations.
enrichment.ratio: Post-writ contractual interest may be claimed against a guarantor without treating him as a principal debtor; where amendment would decide the real dispute without prejudice beyond paying what was contractually due, late amendment should be allowed despite delay.
legal_issues: Whether contractual compound interest could be recovered against a guarantor sued as surety
Whether a debt must be ascertained at writ date
Whether late amendment should be refused for delay or loss of discretionary interest abatement
Whether the second action was an abuse after refusal in the first
linked_authorities: Toepfer v Cremer [1975] 2 Lloyd's Rep 118
Hendry v Chartsearch Ltd [1998] CLC 1382
Maridive and Oil Services (SAE) v CNA Insurance Co (Europe) Ltd [2002] EWCA Civ 369

notes: Assault PC appeal; PACE s.2 stop-and-search non-compliance vitiated execution of duty.

enrichment.short_title: Bonner v DPP: assault PC after unlawful drugs search commencement
key_facts: Plain-clothes officers approached Mr Bonner in Bristol intending a drugs search and revealed body armour but did not produce warrant cards or give section 2 information.
They seized his arms to detain him for search before any PACE-compliant steps or Code A cooperation were attempted.
A struggle followed in which officers and the appellant were injured; the justices convicted him of assaulting a constable in execution of duty.
Both officers accepted breaches of section 2 and Code A paragraph 3.2.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from magistrates' conviction for assaulting a constable in the execution of his duty.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and conviction quashed; the officers were not acting in execution of their duty when the assault occurred.
enrichment.ratio: Where officers contemplate a Misuse of Drugs Act search they must comply with section 2 of PACE before commencing it; failure to do so renders subsequent force unlawful and removes the section 89(1) protection, following Osman v DPP.
legal_issues: Whether section 2 PACE applies before force is used to detain for a drugs search
Whether officers were acting in execution of duty despite personal safety concerns
Whether Code A paragraph 3.2 permitted immediate use of force
Correct formulation of the case stated question
linked_authorities: Osman v DPP (1999) 163 JP 725

confidence.notes: Findings of fact and direct application of Osman make the outcome clear.

notes: Generator exciter failure trial; migration cause upheld and late Regan evidence excluded.

enrichment.short_title: British Sugar v Cegelec: exciter failure and late witness exclusion
key_facts: A steam turbine exciter at British Sugar's Wissington factory failed in September 1996 after a March 1996 repair for winding migration using the old rather than revised design.
The only competing causes were rotor end-winding migration or broken heat sink fins; liability turned on which was proved on the balance of probabilities.
The judge found migration caused the failure and that broken fins occurred during dismantling, not operation.
On day two of trial the judge refused late evidence from operations manager Mr Regan supporting a new heat sink theory disclosed only days earlier.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Technology and Construction Court liability judgment and an interlocutory ruling excluding late lay/expert evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on merits and on the procedural ground; migration was the established cause and exclusion of Mr Regan's late evidence was a lawful case-management decision.
enrichment.ratio: Where only two causation theories exist and the defendant's pleaded theory fails, claimants succeed if migration is more likely; a trial judge may refuse very late evidence supporting a theory internally known for years but disclosed on the eve of trial when it would cause prejudice and delay.
legal_issues: Whether rotor end-winding migration or broken heat sink fins caused the exciter failure
Whether VPI rewinding using the 1991 design breached the repair contract
Whether the judge erred in excluding Mr Regan's evidence
Whether the heat sink fin theory was supported by expert evidence

confidence.notes: Detailed fact findings and separate procedural ruling are both clearly reasoned.

notes: MHRT conditional discharge conditions quashed as inevitable deprivation of liberty.

enrichment.short_title: R (SSHD) v MHRT: unlawful conditional discharge conditions for restricted patient
key_facts: MP is a restricted patient detained since 1976 for manslaughter of an 11-year-old boy, with a history of sadistic paedophilic offending.
The Mental Health Review Tribunal provisionally directed conditional discharge deferred until secure accommodation and 24-hour escort arrangements were in place.
Conditions required residence in staffed secure accommodation from which he could not leave without an escort and constant escort in the community.
The Secretary of State challenged the conditions as inevitably amounting to deprivation of liberty; MP had consented to them.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim to quash a tribunal decision provisionally directing deferred conditional discharge subject to restrictive conditions.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; the residence and escort conditions would inevitably deprive MP of liberty and were beyond the tribunal's power, and patient consent did not render them lawful.
enrichment.ratio: A mental health tribunal may not impose conditional discharge conditions that inevitably amount to deprivation rather than restriction of liberty; conditions imposed primarily to prevent unsupervised access to potential victims are not saved by patient consent.
legal_issues: Whether proposed residence and escort conditions amounted to deprivation of liberty
Whether the tribunal had power to defer conditional discharge on those conditions
Whether patient consent could legitimise unlawful conditions
Distinction from the PH case on purpose and risk profile

MP v Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Trust [2003] EWHC 1782 (Admin)
R(H) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] 3 WLR 1278

notes: RAF reservist AWOL appeal; Article 9 does not excuse conscientious objection following Sepet.

enrichment.short_title: Khan v RAF: Muslim reservist AWOL and Article 9 conscientious objection
key_facts: Leading Aircraftsman Khan, a Muslim medical assistant reservist, was recalled in January 2003 before the Iraq invasion and went absent without leave citing conscientious objection.
The summary appeal court accepted his objection as genuine but held it was no defence; he was sentenced to seven days loss of privileges.
Recall papers listed grounds to revoke call-up but did not expressly mention religion or conscience, though they included compassionate grounds.
He had previously voluntarily enlisted and been discharged on premature voluntary release in 2001.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from the RAF summary appeal court to the Divisional Court on Article 9 ECHR challenges to AWOL conviction and recall procedure.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Article 9 did not provide a defence to AWOL following Sepet, and recall information was sufficient so there was no breach at recall.
enrichment.ratio: Following Sepet, Article 9 does not confer a right to refuse compulsory military service on grounds of conscience or religion and therefore cannot provide a defence to absence without leave; omission of explicit conscientious objection wording in recall papers did not breach Article 9 where compassionate grounds were identified and no relevant manifestation was interfered with.
legal_issues: Whether genuine conscientious objection is a defence to AWOL under Article 9
Whether RAF authorities breached Article 9 by omitting conscientious objection from recall information
Application of Sepet and Thlimmenos to service discipline proceedings
Whether recall, arrest and prosecution interfered with manifestation of belief
linked_authorities: Sepet v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] UKHL 15
Thlimmenos v Greece (ECtHR, 4 December 1998)

confidence.notes: Case stated questions and explicit answers on both Article 9 issues are recorded.
